analysis.one_liner: Terminates Medicare's competitive bidding program for home medical equipment and replaces it with a redesigned auction program.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 180 cosponsors — 131 Republicans and 49 Democrats — but never received a committee markup or floor vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare had been paying for wheelchairs, oxygen, hospital beds, and diabetic supplies through a competitive bidding program that pushed payment rates sharply down. This bill would end that program, temporarily pay suppliers modestly reduced fee-schedule rates, and set up a new "market pricing" auction system designed with outside auction experts. Because the new program would produce higher prices than competitive bidding, the bill rescinds unobligated non-defense domestic spending to stay budget neutral.
analysis.who_benefits: Home medical equipment suppliers and manufacturers. Competitive bidding awarded contracts only to low bidders at rock-bottom prices; this bill would terminate those contracts and the program itself, guarantee payment rates only 5 to 25 percent below the old fee schedule during a transition, let any qualified supplier participate by accepting the auction price, and permanently exclude complex rehabilitative wheelchairs, skin protection cushions, and Class III medical devices from pricing altogether.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home medical equipment suppliers and manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the competitive acquisition program on December 31, 2013, ends all further bidding rounds, and cancels existing competitive bidding contracts as of July 1, 2013, with any resulting damages paid from the Medicare trust fund.

During the transition, suppliers of round 2 items would be paid 95 percent of the old fee schedule, reduced further in 2014 and 2015, and diabetic testing suppliers would be paid 90 percent — cuts far smaller than the prices competitive bidding was producing.

Under the new market pricing program, any qualified supplier who accepts the auction-established price would be awarded a contract, so suppliers no longer need to win a bid to serve Medicare patients in an area.

Complex rehabilitative power wheelchairs, skin protection cushions, certain manual wheelchairs, and Class III medical devices are permanently excluded from the pricing program and would keep their existing payment rates.

The bill requires an auction design that is market-based and does not reduce beneficiary access to or quality of equipment, and it creates an auction expert and market monitor to design, oversee, and publicly report on the program.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare taxpayers and beneficiaries, because the replacement program is designed to produce higher payment rates than the competitive bidding program it repeals. To keep the bill budget neutral, it rescinds unobligated balances from all non-defense, non-Veterans Affairs discretionary appropriations, cutting unrelated federal programs to absorb the added Medicare cost.

drawbacks.text: Replacing competitive bidding with the market pricing program means Medicare pays more for the same equipment than it would under the bidding program — which is why the bill needs a budgetary offset at all, rescinding unobligated non-defense discretionary funds to cover the added cost.

The offset comes from unobligated balances of every non-defense, non-VA discretionary account, so other federal programs — not the equipment industry — absorb the cost of higher Medicare equipment prices.

Even supporters acknowledged the transitional rates still cut supplier payments 5 to 25 percent below the old fee schedule, and the industry's stated concern was that reduced rates could shrink the number of suppliers serving beneficiaries, particularly in rural areas.
The bill bars administrative or judicial review of any claim to enjoin a market-priced auction, so suppliers could not go to court to stop the auctions from going forward.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's dominant effect is to shield home medical equipment suppliers from the lowest prices Medicare had ever paid through competitive bidding, and to fund that protection by rescinding unrelated domestic spending. The redesigned auction addressed real, documented flaws in how CMS ran its bidding program — bid information problems that discouraged participation — and the access safeguards and monitoring are well constructed. But weighed honestly, the bill mainly converts a program that was producing deep price savings into one that pays suppliers more, with the difference made up by cutting other programs.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2013, the bill was referred to three House committees and their health subcommittees, but none of them ever scheduled a markup or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Price (R-GA) introduced the bill on April 24, 2013, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Democrats John Larson, Mike Thompson, and Bruce Braley.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Appropriations Committees.
In late April and early June 2013, the bill was referred to the health subcommittees of Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.
It gathered 180 cosponsors — 131 Republicans and 49 Democrats — but no committee ever reported it, and no floor vote ever occurred.
The bill's last recorded action was the June 3, 2013 subcommittee referral; the 113th Congress ended January 3, 2015 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers are better off, because the existing competitive bidding program — which was producing the lowest equipment prices Medicare had achieved — remained in place, and no unrelated domestic programs were rescinded to pay for higher equipment prices. Suppliers who would have faced continued competitive bidding lost the relief this bill offered.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines — 131 Republicans and 49 Democrats — though support skewed Republican; no floor vote ever tested where the parties actually stood.

industries.note: The bill repeals the competitive bidding program that had driven Medicare's equipment prices to their lowest levels and replaces it with an auction design plus transitional rates only 5-25 percent below the old fee schedule, letting any qualified supplier serve Medicare by accepting the auction price. The suppliers' gain comes directly from Medicare paying more than the bidding program would have paid — a cost borne by taxpayers.

industries.industry: Suppliers of excluded items (complex rehabilitative wheelchairs, skin protection cushions, Class III devices)
industries.note: These suppliers are permanently carved out of the pricing program and keep their existing, higher payment rates, at Medicare's expense.
